overview: Mentions were mostly members citing Auditor-General reports in debate. Report 9 of 2025 supplied state debt figures in November 2025. Report 7 of 2026 prompted questions on North Adelaide Golf Course consultancies, T2D and hydrogen turbines, mainly in question time and the Auditor-General's Report examinations of 27 to 29 October 2026. The Government Advertising Bill proposed an Auditor-General approval role. Road maintenance, a rural industry fund and Coober Pedy council also drew on audit findings, and several reports were tabled.

issues.label: North Adelaide Golf Course consultancy procurement
issues.note: Members cited findings on 14 consultancy contracts under $55,000 and later extensions; the Premier said stage 1 spending was within its $45 million budget.

issues.label: Major project costs: T2D, hydrogen turbines, hospital
issues.note: Questions on T2D overspend and contract management, unsold hydrogen turbines and hospital start delays; ministers pointed to positive findings and cash flow explanations.

issues.label: State debt and budget overspends
issues.note: Members cited Auditor-General warnings that net debt will near $50 billion, and said the Audit Office was the only agency within budget.

issues.label: Government Advertising Bill and Auditor-General's powers
issues.note: Debate on a bill giving the Auditor-General breach investigation and pre-election approval powers, which the government opposed; also special investigations and Joint Parliamentary Service access.

issues.label: Road maintenance backlog and spending
issues.note: Members cited the Auditor-General's reporting of a $2.1 billion road repair estimate and backlog growth, and disputed which government is responsible.

issues.label: Idle Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund
issues.note: Members cited the Auditor-General's figure of $28.4 million in the fund, said to be idle for a decade, during debate on the loan interest bill.

debates.gist: Committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report, with members citing report pages to question ministers on the Concordia infrastructure scheme, SA Water contract management, the Eyre Peninsula desalination budget, CFS records and Women's and Children's Hospital timing.

Second reading debate on the Government Advertising Bill 2026. The government opposed it as duplicating existing safeguards, including the Auditor-General's audit power; supporters backed the Auditor-General approving election-period advertising above $10,000 as an independent safeguard.

Committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report, covering DHS agreements and NDIS billing, surplus cash returned to Treasury, removal of audit of procurement disclosures, and the Auditor-General's procurement-risk concerns about alliance subcontractors.

House motion on road maintenance. Members cited the Auditor-General's note of a $2.1 billion repair estimate, depreciation exceeding maintenance spending and backlog figures since 2018, while disputing which government is responsible.

Committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report, with the Premier asked about North Adelaide Golf Course consultancy contracts and Treasurer's Instruction 17, the Treasurer on concurrent employment across agencies, and ministers on bank guarantees, SmartyGrants security controls and Veterans SA expenses.

Second reading debate on a bill on Coober Pedy council. Members recounted that the former Ombudsman's report and a later Auditor-General's examination, finalised in late 2018, identified maladministration and financial governance failings that led to the council's administration.

Legislative Council committee examination of the 2024-25 Auditor-General's Report, after a motion to refer it. Questions covered the Victims of Crime Fund balance, the AGFMA contract with Ventia, a CAA payroll database issue, and PIRSA drought funding and expenditure.

House of Assembly committee examination of the 2024-25 Auditor-General's Report: SA Housing Trust maintenance backlog and IT controls, child protection expenses and payments, and CFS PPC cleaning compliance, with some findings said to be repeated from earlier years.

SA-0001.summary: Opened the committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report, requiring questions to reference the report and agency statements, and called Mr Teague, who began with Part C on the Concordia Basic Infrastructure Scheme (page 235).

SA-0002.summary: Began a question citing Auditor-General's Report 7 of 2026, following an answer about code amendments, infrastructure overlays and infrastructure schemes; the excerpt ends before the question itself.

SA-0003.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's note of higher 2025-26 transaction volumes, asking whether transfer fees will fall; then cited concerns about SA Water contract and risk management for strategic contracts, asking what is done to ensure contractor and subcontractor probity.

SA-0004.summary: Said the Auditor-General's engagement with SA Water concerned documentation and procedural issues that SA Water has taken on board and is implementing; Mr Telfer then asked whether the Eyre Peninsula desalination plant remains within its $470 million budget.

SA-0005.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's commentary at page 355 on the Eyre Peninsula desalination plant and its $470 million budget, asking whether the project is on track or will incur additional costs, and how much.

SA-0006.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's finding that most CFS PPC improvement initiatives were not fully implemented and records incomplete, questioning another external audit after four years of shortcomings; separately cited 44 SES fleet assets with no service record, asking how the minister reconciles that with everything being operational.

SA-0007.summary: Said the delay noted at page 99 of the Auditor-General's Report reflects a change in spending phasing after project realignment, not a late construction start, and cited Part A's list of 2025-26 milestones on the new Women's and Children's Hospital.

SA-0008.summary: Asked whether the minister disagrees with the Auditor-General's assessment of delays in starting construction on the hospital project; the minister replied that the underspend is a cash flow issue, not a project delay.

SA-0009.summary: Said the government will oppose the Government Advertising Bill 2026, arguing it duplicates existing safeguards, including the Auditor-General's power under the Public Finance and Audit Act 1987 to audit government advertising and report to parliament.

SA-0010.summary: Argued that the bill's role for the Auditor-General in assessing breaches and approving pre-election advertising above $10,000 is an important feature, giving an independent mechanism to enforce the rules and report to parliament.

SA-0011.summary: Supported the bill's restrictions on government advertising, describing the Auditor-General's oversight of spending above $10,000 in the pre-election period as an important safeguard against misuse of public funds for political advantage.

SA-0012.summary: Claimed Labor introduced a near-identical bill in 2021 while in opposition, requiring Auditor-General or parliamentary approval of election-period advertising above $10,000, and argued this shows inconsistency on accountability now it is in government.

SA-0013.summary: Argued the bill makes the Auditor-General, an independent statutory officer appointed by parliament, the arbiter of whether taxpayer-funded advertising is necessary for the functions of government, and called that wholly appropriate.

SA-0014.summary: Opened the committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report; Mr Batty began with page 238 of Part C, citing 68 agreements that had expired in DHS's system in June 2026.

SA-0015.summary: Cited Auditor-General's Report 7 of 2026 on $58 million in surplus cash returned to Treasury, asking whether any related to seniors and ageing well funding and why it was unspent, then asked about the algal bloom event support package.

SA-0016.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's calls for improved NDIS billing policies and procedures in 2023-24 and 2024-25, and asked why DHS was still considering an overarching NDIS billing policy in 2025-26 and what progress has been made.

SA-0017.summary: Cited Part A, page 37, noting the Auditor-General modified several agencies' audit opinions in 2023-24 and 2024-25 over incomplete procurement disclosures, and asked whether the minister agreed to remove audit of that information.

SA-0018.summary: Said the department will keep building on the Auditor-General's recommendations, noted a further audit this year and thanked the Auditor-General for diligent work, and said the alliance is a separate legal entity from DIT.

SA-0019.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's procurement-risk concern about subcontracts at page 28, after the Chair asked for closer reference to the report, and asked what power the government exercises if it is not party to them.

SA-0020.summary: Moved a motion for documents on North Adelaide Golf Course contracts, citing the Auditor-General's findings that 14 consultants were engaged at under $55,000 without competitive procurement, then 11 extended above that, and arguing the government lacks transparency.

SA-0021.summary: Supported the golf course motion for the Greens, citing the Auditor-General's report as showing the government avoided scrutiny of Parklands plans and funded the project without a clear business case; claimed the same happened with the university merger.

SA-0022.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's June 2025 report on proton therapy project funding ($115.4 million committed, about $98.5 million spent) and its finding that the government could not show PwC's concerns about the operating model were adequately assessed.

SA-0023.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's note of a 2023 departmental estimate that $2.1 billion was needed to repair roads in very poor condition, and argued five-year road depreciation of $1.8 billion exceeded the $884 million spent on maintenance.

SA-0024.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's documentation that the maintenance backlog was $750 million when the Liberals took government in 2018 and almost $2 billion when they left, and challenged the opposition's account.

SA-0025.summary: Cited the RAA's November 2025 assessment of the Auditor-General's Report that five-year road depreciation of $1.6 billion exceeded maintenance spending of $892 million, a 45 per cent shortfall, and called for a funded recovery plan.

SA-0026.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report of a $2.1 billion 2023 departmental estimate to repair roads in very poor condition, and claimed the Auditor-General has said for 4½ years that the department has not managed the road maintenance contract correctly.

SA-0027.summary: Cited the Auditor-General for the figure of about $28.4 million remaining in the Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund, while arguing primary industries, especially wine, face significant structural pressures.

SA-0028.summary: Asked, in a question put on 3 September 2026, whether the Auditor-General undertook a special investigation in 2025-26, whether none is expected in 2026-27, and when the Auditor-General last did not undertake one.

SA-0029.summary: Answered for the Premier that the Auditor-General undertook no special investigation in 2025-26, saying such investigations are uncommon, arise only on a formal request or requirement under the Public Finance and Audit Act 1987, and cannot be predicted.

SA-0030.summary: Opened the committee examination of the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report with the Premier, where Mrs Hurn asked why 14 North Adelaide Golf Course consultancy contracts were each under $55,000; later, asked how much contractors had been paid, the Premier cited $15.6 million against $45 million approved for stage 1.

SA-0031.summary: Opened questioning of the Premier on the Auditor-General's 2025-26 Report by citing the Executive Summary's identification of the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment as a key matter, asking why 14 consultancy contracts were all valued under $55,000.

SA-0032.summary: Said compliance with Treasurer's Instruction 17 was achieved through approvals in a cabinet submission the Auditor-General may not have seen, and that cabinet's practice is to consider and, where it can, comply with the Auditor-General's requests for such information.

SA-0033.summary: Opened questioning of the Treasurer on Part A of Report 7 of 2026, then quoted the Auditor-General on workers employed by multiple agencies: '...did not assess whether the concurrent employment arrangements were justified, appropriately approved, complied with relevant policies or suitable' given workload and wellbeing.

SA-0034.summary: Said agencies must manage fatigue for staff working across agencies and that the Auditor-General's report helps identify the issue, adding that the extra hours reflect people taking weekend work during a cost-of-living crisis.

SA-0035.summary: Cited Report 7 of 2026, page 81, on $418 million in bank guarantees held as security, and asked what rehabilitation security was held for projects in Narungga at 30 June 2026.

SA-0036.summary: Responded to the Auditor-General's finding that the Department of State Development had not defined how often to monitor SmartyGrants vendor security controls, describing the cloud-based grants system as used since 2022 and holding sensitive applicant information.

SA-0037.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Report as showing Veterans SA employee expenses rose by about 11.7 per cent and asked what additional services or measurable improvements for veterans resulted; the Chair asked which part of the report was cited.

SA-0038.summary: Recounted that Coober Pedy council was placed into administration in January 2019 on the basis of reports by the former Ombudsman and later the Auditor-General, citing findings of maladministration over a power purchasing agreement and significant financial governance failings.

SA-0039.summary: Said the Ombudsman's findings on Coober Pedy council were supported by a lengthy Auditor-General examination, finalised in late 2018, that identified significant financial governance failings, and noted the council is uniquely responsible for essential services in the town.

SA-0040.summary: Said a pattern of serious mismanagement at Coober Pedy council was shown by the former Ombudsman's report and a later Auditor-General's report, including maladministration of a power purchasing agreement, and called the decision to place it into administration necessary.
